for_you_if: you enjoy deep sandbox survival loops

Too unintuitive and boring. Game wants me to cook some fruit but in order to find out how, I need to go through all menus until I randomly find it. Game mentions a "status" thing on the radial menu - there's no such button. Aside from that, it's just boring, I cba to slowly walk around trying to hit a rabbit with a stone. Story seems interesting but it's just no fun to play at all - I guess that's how people liked their survival games 12 years ago.

when a game can't tell the difference between difficulty through tough choices, delicate balance/management of ressources/status, skills and difficulty through "I'm not telling you anything, I'm giving your zero clue about what action does what, how much time you actually have left, how much time that action will take, etc..." and you just have to save scum and redo things again and again and again in the first hour of the game, there's a problem. I guess I could go google it but like... really? That's your game? 
I guess some players like it, idk, but as far as I'm concerned it's crap and fells pretty uninspired.
Now add to that an overall feeling of clunkiness (which I would have been ok with if it was just that) and lack of precision in the interactions - which is particularly annoying when the it's same button between "interact with" and "action/shoot" and you end up throwing away a stone when what you actually wanted to do is pick up a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stunned rabbit which litteraly goes back up right away and escapes when you don't have time for this sh*t.
I wanted to love this game, story driven survival with a nice nostalgia vibe sounded really nice. But damn the gameplay is just bad and takes you out of it. Quite disapointed. :s
I think this game is basically a walking sim right of the bat spawn in die over and over on easy mode and no clear direction given.

Have you ever thought, "Man, I wish Minecraft was super realistic, set in Canada, and was as difficult as DarkSouls"?

Well, The Long Dark thought that for you and made it happen.

This game hates you if you want it to and challenges you to survive with almost no guidance. Its the abusive relationship your friends and family try to get you out of, only for you to keep going back because "it'll be different this time, I'll change my behavior and they'll do the same". No, they wont. But do it anyway. The gameplay is awesome, smooth, and immersive. The mechanics are harsh but clear and straightforward. The world is vast and worth inching yourself through. Each accomplishment feels deeply satisfying and rewarding. I played the normal survival on like barely the lowest level and this game was relentlessly unforgiving until I got my ♥♥♥♥ together, and I loved it.

If you like the survival, solo games where you have to learn through trial and error, this is your shtick. If you're curious about the genre, get it and try it out. There's plenty of modes to accommodate any gamer play style and vibe.

cohorts.summary: Surviving requires managing vital stats through dark nights and harsh conditions, while the campaign introduces a structured narrative alongside the sandbox.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game world as dark at night, making it difficult to see or perform activities until morning.

citations.review_text: Appropriately named title, I spent a LONG time sitting in the DARK waiting to be able to see anything in order to do any playing.

I really want to like this game. It has gotten great updates over the years and I have played some amount everytime hoping they would make it more fun to play. In nature survival games can be a bit boring to play but this has got so many great things going on that I am conflicted in my review. The scenery, graphics, music, sounds, mechanics are genuinely good. The major gripe I have with the game is night time. When its night you can not see anything, its pitch black. Which means until is morning you can not search for items, you can not make fires because you can not see anything. During daytime and when you have light the game feels great to play but during night time its so unbalanced and frustrating experience it turns me off everytime.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the story mode, Wintermute, declines in quality or has frustrating elements in its later episodes.

citations.review_text:
Been a fond enjoyer of the Long Dark game for quite a long time, having played mostly on Xbox. Survival Mode is of course great as always, and would recommend playing it. However, the WINTERMUTE Story Mode turned sour, and would very much not recommend it due to Episode 5. It was good in my opinion, for the first 3 episodes mainly. But somehow, after waiting all this time for Episode 5, it was a spit in the face. 
Take this as you will.

I started playing this game years ago, way back when storymode is not a thing. the story for episode 1 and 2 was really cool back then, it was really good. 3 and 4 was great too, but they stopped as "personal beef" between a group of convicts and some people trying hard to survive.
Then episode 5 came, it was my most waited thing, i was so hyped for it, i bought this game on steam just to pay the dev some tribute. 
Turns out this episode has the most ♥♥♥♥ story ive ever played, devs said they need time to polish things, trying to deliver us the greatest experience, a grand boom. nah nah they are lying.
So so so many plot holes, from personal beefs all of a sudden expanded to a worldwide threat, molly and jeremiah all of a sudden appear in the scene, you yourself have a shotgun, a rifle, a revoler, a ballistic vest, basically a walking armory, then boom all of your stuff disappear in the final bits. devs really dont want us to kill the convicts, then someone we walk straight back to the lion's den to make a message that you arent sure if it will goes out or not. Reason? to have that tear jerking final scene between astrid and mackenzie (its so ass it just turned me off completely)
So many bugs unfixed in the story, so many unjustified "take away your stuffs". Atp i wont even buy TLD2 or Blackfrost, so many delay just to be served slop. 
So much slop i have to went out of my way to write a review.
PUT THE FRIES IN THE BAG ATP.
Survival mode is fantastic, im at 18 hours on pc, and 250 hours on xbox. wintermute on the other hand is garbage. dont waste your money or time

I like the survival mode a lot. I recently migrated from playing this game on console to playing on pc, so my hours are not accurate.

Score: 9/10

The Long Dark is one of the most immersive survival games ever made. Instead of zombies, mutants, or constant combat, the real enemy is the frozen Canadian wilderness. Every decision matters: finding food, staying warm, avoiding wolves, and managing limited supplies.

What it does well

✅ Atmosphere

The game excels at making you feel isolated and vulnerable.
Snowstorms, howling winds, and abandoned cabins create a unique sense of loneliness.

✅ Survival Mechanics

Hunger, thirst, fatigue, temperature, and injuries all need attention.
Resources are scarce, making every matchstick and can of food valuable.

✅ Exploration

Large interconnected regions reward careful exploration.
Discovering a remote cabin after barely surviving a blizzard feels genuinely satisfying.

✅ Art Style

Uses a stylized, painterly look rather than realistic graphics.
The visuals have aged very well because of this choice.
Weaknesses

❌ Slow Pace

Players expecting action may find it boring.
Much of the game involves walking, planning, and resource management.

❌ Learning Curve

New players often die repeatedly before understanding the survival systems.

❌ Wildlife AI

Wolves and bears can sometimes feel predictable or frustrating rather than realistic.
Game Modes
Survival Mode – The main sandbox experience where you survive as long as possible.
Wintermute – A story campaign with characters, quests, and narrative.
Challenges – Special scenarios with unique objectives.
Who will enjoy it?

You'll probably love The Long Dark if you enjoy:

Project Zomboid
Green Hell
Subnautica
Slow, methodical survival gameplay
Exploration and resource management

You may not enjoy it if you prefer:

Fast-paced action
Frequent combat
Multiplayer (the game is primarily single-player)
Verdict

The Long Dark creates stories naturally. Surviving a blizzard with no food, reaching a cabin just before freezing to death, or hearing wolves nearby whi…

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features a slow pace centered around walking, resource management, and survival mechanics.

citations.review_text: If a slow death march to no where sounds like fun to you then this is your game. Not mine. I really wanted to like this game, but after several tries I felt cheated and honestly bored. I really like survival games, but this one is just certain pointless death with no interesting game. There should be some strategy or point to efforts, but there seems to be none. Everything hinges on finding a cooking pot which seems rare fro some reason. The last straw for me was when I finally had plenty of food, water and shelter, I just died for no apparent reason when I went to bed fed and hydrated. No saves without going to sleep is also a sad lack of feature for the game. Graphics are not good. You can't jump or climb so obstacles knee high end up being impassible barriers. Graphics are really bad. It's mostly a constant slog of a boring, boring march unless you're in the right location which there are few and then the game kills you randomly with no apparent cause anyway. And the graphics are absolutely terrible! Just abysmal.

It's classy and has great music, but... it's just so much work to do anything, I don't want to keep playing. Every move you make drains your heat, food and water, so you have to ♥♥♥♥ around taking care of that. It becomes one giant chore and combined with the slow movement, playing is a slog and not much fun. The story is intriguing, but everyone talks SO SLOWLY it takes forever to get anything worthwhile - and frankly it's just not good enough to endure the "game" to find out more. I'd rather just read a good book.

I'm still giving it a thumbs up because of how well it's made, but you really need a high tolerance for survival mechanisms to actually enjoy it.

cohorts.label: 20-100h
cohorts.summary: Extended playtime exposes demanding survival loops, terrain obstacles, and technical problems with save files alongside slow campaign pacing.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the survival mode can feel slow, challenging, and punishing, requiring methodical planning and patience.

citations.review_text: A survival game that I keep coming back to! Story mode is good for beginners and the story itself, although currently unfinished, keeps you hooked. Survival mode can be slow and challenging at first, but once you find your groove it's one of the best survival games out there, imo. It takes a lot of time and effort to craft the things you want to craft, do the things that you want to do, and survive. There are lots of different elements at play, interesting and unique game mechanics, and lots to keep track of. You truly feel alone in a vast, sometimes desolate winterscape, with only yourself, your supplies, and your skills to rely on. 10/10.

This survival game has a special place in my heart over the others of its kind. Unlike many, it veers away from the idea of instant gratification or conventional "drops". Many materials must be properly treated or air dried for use, which means your advance often requires methodical planning. It rewards migration from several different areas to others in order to keep a reliable amount of supplies at hand. 

Although this kind of gameplay might be too "slow" for some, I greatly enjoy it. Mistakes are extremely punishing, and caution is often rewarded over risk-taking. It also gives a eeriely haunting experience to be in a snowy wasteland where you can tell people once lived, trapped in a winter that never ends.

tldr; my favorite survival game. Highly recomended.  Instilled a deep seated fear of Moose in me.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that navigating terrain involves getting stuck on minor obstacles like tiny branches on the ground.

citations.review_text:
Ill mostly focus on Wintermute episode 5

ignore to avoid spoilers



Everyone bashing Episode 5 I think has some valid criticism, stuff cut like detail animations to dialogue being rushed sometimes and being cheesy/out of character is mostly due to the 3 team split between Hinterlands Survival, wintermute, and blackfrost teams. I enjoyed Part 1 even though there were no side quests because I was invested in the mystery at least, I know most people will whine and complain how linear it is. I DO NOT MIND IT at all, there were a lot of loose ends from Episode 4 that needed to be tied up as quickly as possible. The parts I do hate come in part two as soon as the cable car section hit. There were some stupid logic points over there, and the wintermute devs explaining it as "its what it shows that mack will do anything to help people" which has already been gone over in episode 1-2 and 4 is redundant. The mines were corny still, but when I got to szuki it was a breath of... slightly fresh air. The timed mission was stressful, and I think more time was needed fleshing it out but otherwise it was alright... The exposition, even if people bash it for being "oooo this is how the lights workkkk ooo so scary" exposition I don't really care. The explanation is needed for those who want answers, and for some bonus information, even in the monologue they know its too long and they cut it down slightly. I was invested in Wintermute's backstory and the dialogue between the two, it felt a return to connection between everyone there. 

The rest I enjoyed pretty much as swell as I could. I know people complain about Jeremiah and Molly returning suddenly, but if you can at least piece it together and stop moping over the cable cart (like I did) you can realize that they moved on as quickly as they could from ML and PV due to Jeremiah's connection to Atwood, and Molly having a potential reason to follow them to PM. 

While I don't fully approve of the weird "Mack running off with the pr…

I couldn’t finish the second chapter. It’s insanely boring. Roughly 90% of it is just walking. I’d turn on auto-walk and sit there for tens of minutes, just watching the character trudge along. The first chapter had some momentum; the second one I couldn’t endure. Everything the protagonist does is painfully slow. The final straw was when I was walking at night with a lamp, got attacked by a wolf, tried to switch to a weapon, and while he took his sweet time turning off the light and drawing it, I got eaten.

After you take damage — an injury, an incident — you have to open the menu and figure out how to treat it by the icon. I repeat, by the icon. You can’t simply apply a remedy from a list. You go to the status screen, look at the little icon indicating what’s wrong (bandage, antibiotics, painkillers, mushroom tea, whatever), then go into your inventory and manually select the item you think matches. It’s perfectly normal to accidentally take antibiotics instead of painkillers, or brew the wrong tea, only for the game to tell you “that didn’t do anything.”

The game is a pain. It’s interesting for a few hours, but then it becomes a constant battle with bad UI, bad UX, and endless walking. And the walking itself isn’t polished. Sometimes you don’t even know what’s stopping you — the protagonist gets caught on a tiny branch five centimetres high and can’t step over it.

I haven’t even started on the plot, but I’ll give it this: I admire the main character’s self-reflection. I like that he realises nothing makes sense. I don’t like that he never acts on that understanding. He thinks nothing makes sense, yet behaves as if it does.

Visuals: 7/10
Gameplay: 3/10
Plot: 2/10

I bought the game around 2017, right after it left early access, and it was okay-ish back then. Now, in 2026, it’s just outdated and boring. Don’t buy.

Sorry, Hinterland.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the story mode features long cutscenes and slow pacing, with early episodes feeling drawn out or repetitive.

citations.review_text:
Questa recensione è su WINTERMUTE, la storymode. I primi 2-3 episodi sono molto densi, poi procede diventando più lineare con meno side, aumentano e si allungano le cutscene.
I personaggi non sono particolarmente approfonditi ma è il contesto di fondo che la fa da padrone. Il mistero dell'aurora viene gradualmente ma non pienamente spiegato nell'ultimo episodio che chiude comunque l'arco narrativo in modo piacevole. 
Per un nuovo player completare prima Wintermute e poi giocare survival è sensato sia per come si chiude la storia sia perché nel corso delle attività coprite tutta la mappa, permettendo in survival di sapere almeno a grandi linee che tipo di troverete e quando distanti saranno rispetto a dove vi trovate.
Il problema principale dello story mode è che dilatato in attività da ripetere praticamente tutte tre volte.
Devi fare una determinata quest? E' splittata in tre attività uguali da ripetere in posti diversi, praticamente tutte così.
A 'na certa magari uno si rompe pure il cazzo.
In story mode però il gioco aiuta molto, l'aspetto survival è limitato fondamentalmente alla gestione del vestiario, durabilità armi e sonno, per il resto ti tira dietro cibo preconfezionato, proiettili, oggetti, farmaci eccetera.
Conoscerete perfettamente la mappa ma la modalità survival è tutta un'altra bestia.
Vale comunque la pena completare lo story mode anche in relazione del futuro seguito, che mi auguro sarà meno ripetitivo ed abbia un crafting più avanzato rispetto a Wintermute.

[b][i]Episodes 1 and 2 feel drawn out[/i][/b] – The pacing in these early chapters can be slow.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game as heavily reliant on walking and traveling long distances across the map.

citations.review_text: the game moves to slow for my liking, the long walk is not recommended for people who watches tiktok, your attention span is not gonna last on this game

I couldn’t finish the second chapter. It’s insanely boring. Roughly 90% of it is just walking. I’d turn on auto-walk and sit there for tens of minutes, just watching the character trudge along. The first chapter had some momentum; the second one I couldn’t endure. Everything the protagonist does is painfully slow. The final straw was when I was walking at night with a lamp, got attacked by a wolf, tried to switch to a weapon, and while he took his sweet time turning off the light and drawing it, I got eaten.

After you take damage — an injury, an incident — you have to open the menu and figure out how to treat it by the icon. I repeat, by the icon. You can’t simply apply a remedy from a list. You go to the status screen, look at the little icon indicating what’s wrong (bandage, antibiotics, painkillers, mushroom tea, whatever), then go into your inventory and manually select the item you think matches. It’s perfectly normal to accidentally take antibiotics instead of painkillers, or brew the wrong tea, only for the game to tell you “that didn’t do anything.”

The game is a pain. It’s interesting for a few hours, but then it becomes a constant battle with bad UI, bad UX, and endless walking. And the walking itself isn’t polished. Sometimes you don’t even know what’s stopping you — the protagonist gets caught on a tiny branch five centimetres high and can’t step over it.

I haven’t even started on the plot, but I’ll give it this: I admire the main character’s self-reflection. I like that he realises nothing makes sense. I don’t like that he never acts on that understanding. He thinks nothing makes sense, yet behaves as if it does.

Visuals: 7/10
Gameplay: 3/10
Plot: 2/10

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the campaign includes unskippable introductory studio credits and long cutscenes.

citations.review_text: the intro movie in the campaign is unbearable and no way to skip it. guys, i understand this is the accomplishment of your life, but being forced to stare for minutes at an endless list of collaborators and tech people is not what i am paying for. this is one of the hundreds of games in my library. i do not recall the name of any of the developers and engineers of any of them - the same way you do not recall the names of the studio staff of the evening news - it is there on the screen after each news segment.

Wow, its finally finished. After over a decade of development, somehow a DLC storymode being finished first, and a lifecycle that can only be called dev-hell...... What do we have to show for it? Nothing more than we started with. This game is the definition of a neutral rating deserver. 

The base survival elements are still good. They had better be after all, its the only thing that kept this game alive after making all these years. I mean this games dev cycle outlived many peoples dogs. But heres the issue, while it was a good survival game back in the day, today its one of many. So while it continues to be a great survival sandbox mode, its nothing special beyond that.

So that brings me to the coveted story mode, I held off playing chapters 2-5 for a decade after I learned it was episodic as a teenager(now a grown man closing in on 30). I have now binged the game over again to experience it and BOY HOWDY IT WAS NOT WORTH IT. I mean good lord, chapters 1-2 were decent writing, then I can only assume covid or something hit and they lost any ability to write at all. They also decided to remove the ability to skip dialogue, which is great when the characters go on 20 minute long tangents about utter nonsense. Why do I have to listen to this random person I just met talk about their dream for 10 minutes? And because of what I can only assume is a complete in ability to render proper cutscenes in engine, most of these stunningly unskippable cutscenes you are staring at a wall or a blank face. I literally walked my dog and got a cup of coffee and sometimes they still had not shut up. Not to mention every character was reduced to between 3-4 braincells the last 2 chapters. Without spoilers, I will just say these people are so stupid you will scream at the screen. They are genuinely lobotomized. Combine that with the gameplay sequences of the last chapter feeling like your pulling teeth, and you will start to lose your sanity. Then finally you reach the ending after all…

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the survival mode sandbox as deep and endlessly replayable, offering customizable difficulty settings and a strong core gameplay loop focused on exploration and resource management.

citations.review_text: A survival game that doesn't include zombies or cannibalistic humans. It's you against nature, the elements and wildlife. Beautiful graphics, amazing ambience. I found this game back in 2021, so I have both Survival and Story modes, and I bought the DLC. I prefer Survival with the DLC stories for my own gameplay as opposed to Story mode.

Get this game for: relief from a busy and stressful world, peace, beautiful art style, stunning music, endless Survival Mode gameplay possibilities, experiencing a game like no other.

I was fortunate enough to buy The Long Dark early on when Wintermute, Survival Mode, and Tales from The Far Territories were all included. That said, would I buy the full bundle now, even thoigh more expensive? Yes.

Survival Mode is by far the best value for money because you can explore for hours (I'm on over 1000hrs and I've barely scratched the surface of what's possible) and create your own survival story and goals. The experience is massively enhanced by watching some of the most experienced TLD streamers and YouTubers (Bashrobe and Zaknafein are a good starting point) because you get an idea of what's possible. 

The TLD world is somewhere you want to come back to. It's not hyperrealistic but that's what makes it beautiful and calming. You still feel exactly what you are supposed to feel, the colours aren't garish, the music is absolutely beautiful (recommend the soundtrack for Wintermute, also), the sounds are really good.

The solo play, the lack of NPCs, and the lack of zombies or similar, make it a unique and relaxing survival experience. And the difficulty is whatever you choose; it is possible to have a passive exploring experience, a harsher PVE experience, or a custom experience with the perfect mix for you.

Yes, this game has bugs. Most of the bugs are well known and, once you know about them, avoidable. Some are irritating enough for people to have rage quit and uninstalled but I have not had this issue myself. If you play the game, you have to be willing to accept it for what it is. What it is is a game over a decade old, which has become bigger than the devs even realised, and has been made available across multiple platforms, with many updates. Yes, there are bugs and issues. But, overall, it is above and beyond in terms of value for money and enjoyment and the de…

The game closest to The Long Dark I've played so far is Project Zomboid. There are surprisingly many parallels I can think of. One being the same atmospheric, serene solitude. The gameplay is surprisingly similar as well, you spend early-game suffering the most as your skills and loot are all at the lowest point, but progressively as you accumulate gear and skills the game becomes easier and easier until you fully transition from surviving to thriving and then spend most of "late-game" base-building and collecting rare items. There is also a custom sandbox difficulty to craft your perfect world and there are many challenge scenarios for you to change up the gameplay with so a lot of ways to get out of the game what you are looking for.

There are many regions to explore, many resources to gather, many challenges to overcome and many beautiful sights to see. The Far Territories DLC also adds so much content it is absolutely worth the price IMO and the core gameplay loop is very enjoyable and doesn't get repetitive on me as of yet.

The only negatives for me personally are the optional Cougar's respawn mechanics & not earning badge/feat progress in Custom difficulties so until you unlock those you want to make progress towards you may not play the exact version of The Long Dark you'd enjoy the most until you unlock them.

I haven't delved into mods yet so I can't say how easy/difficult it is, but without mods the game is exceptionally stable. No crashes, no freezes, no errors or bugs that I would have noticed so far, except for one - with the Far Territories DLC the cooking interface can sometimes softlock you and you will need to restart the game to fix it.

If I were to nit-pick I will also say I'd prefer the Custom difficulty sliders to be more descriptive in how much they change the game. I can't tell what difference is between "High" and "Very High" and some sliders such as Deer spawn-rate being set to "Low" also seems to not work properly as currently on…

Warning: this will be a detailed review with pros, cons, and loads of text. Also some less obvious tips near the end.

It's righteously considered THE winter survival game, and even after 10 years, the survival mode holds up perfectly.

Let me talk about Wintermute for a moment, then I'll get back to survival; I got both as a bundle on sale, played the first episode as a tutorial, went to survival and never looked back. What I did play was fun, but not for me, and even if you do like story-based games, I heavily recommend looking at Wintermute's reviews first because it seems to have gone off the deep end.


Now, I offer you my impressions of the esteemed survival mode!

PROS:

- multiple difficulties that actually FEEL different, plus a completely custom mode (though you can't earn achievements there)

- said custom mode has loads of customization options, from clothing/tool degradation, to weather, to animal behavior

- many different-looking regions to explore, which, in a game that's mostly white snow and dark rocks, is an accomplishment

- collectibles that keep the game interesting for hours after your character's basic needs have been met

- also a few brutally difficult challenges

- but also opportunities for beautiful screenshots in the calmer moments

- the ability to customize interiors (in a limited way crafting-wise, but there are plenty of decorations you can "borrow")

- AMAZING sound design: I mostly play with passive wildlife for realism, and the music still makes wandering through a snowy forest at night feel tense without even really trying to. There are subtle (and not so subtle) weather cues, animals might let you know if you're getting too close by growling, and you can hear blizzards from inside buildings

- quite realistic animal tracks in the snow (and your own bootprints)

- you can write notes for each day and potentially keep a journal as your survivor, and draw a map with charcoal (though the latter is executed very poorly)

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the final chapters and conclusion of the Wintermute story mode suffer from poor writing, frustrating pacing, and an overreliance on cutscenes and linear scripted sequences.

citations.review_text: Survival mode is fine, however I would not recommend the developers at all. It's taken over a decade to finally finish their game, and the final episode(s) are complete nonsense. The writing is something else, and I don't see this company's poor work ethic improving in the future. The Long Dark survival mode is worth the price, but I wouldn't bother with Wintermute due to the writing

Ok, I certainly recommend this game. I've been playing it since early access in 2015 or so. Finally, I came back to it and finished Wintermute. I generally liked Episodes 1-3. Episode 4 was a bit questionable. But I didn't like Episode 5 at all. Ok, I get it - you need to wrap up the story, but it was like I played a totally different game. 
[spoiler] Cutscene after a cutscene after a cutscene and then QTE after a QTE on top of QTE 
You collect inventory in one episode, its is gone in next one. And then again and again. Sometimes your inventory is even taken from you in the middle of episode :(
[/spoiler]

Still, you should play this game if you like story-rich survival games. 
Can't wait for TLD2!

I can fully recommend the Survival mode of this game. It's very well fleshed out and offers interesting challenges and variety of different areas in the world to explore. If you're looking for a semi realistic crafting survival experience, I would say give that a try. In addition, there's also several challenge scenarios to do for shorter play sessions. I also have to mention that the soundtrack for the entire game is amazing. It does a really good job of making the player feel melancholic or uneasy during tense situations. 

The story mode, Wintermute is a different experience all together. It still has the same survival mechanics but with a story and occasionally interesting and unique mechanics. Also, I'm not sure if it's because it took them years to finish writing the story (maybe writers changed?), but the final 2 chapters are just strangely written and has cutscenes that just annoy me. There's also a 10 minute exposition dump in the final chapter which was really needed but at the same time felt like a cop out way to explain the game (and even the next game's?) premise.

Spoilers for the story: [spoiler] The antagonist, Mathis is a complete nut job that is armed with a hand axe. Multiple times, I've thought, Wow. I have a gun or even multiple guns. Yet we keep ending up in situations where he chokes or knocks our characters out. Or there would be situations where other characters could shoot him yet they don't. It's a bit baffling and in the end.. Mackenzie joins up with him? It's a really frustrating ending that just baffles me with how it was written. [/spoiler]

Despite my gripes with the final chapter, I think the story mode is interesting enough with the mechanics they introduced and the intrigue of why the world is in it's current state.  I just wish the final chapter was written better.

Let's be clear: the survival mode and the first three seasons of Wintermute are the GOAT. Absolutely recommended.

But episodes 4 and 5? Not so much. Episode 5 is especially frustrating. There is literally nothing left of the survival aspect. It’s just a linear fetch-quest with points of interest on an empty map that isn't worth exploring.

The narrative consistency completely falls apart, too. NPCs basically teleport. Where MacKenzie spends days struggling to get somewhere, someone else just breezes through the distance in a couple of hours. The entire plot of the fifth episode, particularly the ending, relies on lazy writing, absurd coincidences, and a whole pantheon of deus ex machina.

It’s a shame, because the first three seasons and survival mode set the bar so high, making these final episodes an incredibly disappointing conclusion.

Survival Mode is great. The story mode, "Wintermute", however, was very much not worth the wait. It could have been great by just using the core gameplay loop of Survival Mode as a base and then putting a story and quests on top of it. Instead, it starts off using [i]some[/i] of the survival mechanics (that we are actually here for), but as it goes on it ditches more and more of them in favor of clichéd setpieces and cutscenes that feel like an eternity - with a total reset in between episodes. And in fact, they reuse so little that not only did they release Survival Mode as a stand-alone game, but each episode of Wintermute is essentially its own game, with subtle differences in code (which is certainly... a choice). Many of the quests are badly designed with unnecessary busywork and poor cluing (and have ever decreasing quality control - the objective description for one of the last quests is, even now, months after release, literally just [i]Lorem Ipsum[/i]).

Well, despite that it could have at least pulled off a great narrative, right? Oh no. Towards the end the writing is [i]aggressively[/i] bad. Think "everything that made the later seasons of [i]The Walking Dead[/i] unwatchable" taken up to 11.

So don't buy the full game. Buy the stand-alone survival mode version of the game that they made. That version is well worth the money. This version isn't.

I have been playing this game off and on for almost 10 years now. I originally played on the Xbox, where I spent hundreds of hours on survival mode. When I moved my gaming to PC, I bought the game again not only to play but to give Hinterland more of my money (which is a rare thing to want to do). They have given me so much enjoyment over the years for such little money, they are truly one of the few studios to still have heart and integrity.

The story mode is nice, especially the first 3 episodes. The reviews saying that episodes 4 and 5 are maybe not as good or felt rushed, I would agree with that. I also wouldn't say that it diminishes the overall substance of the game. Overall, the story is good. That's only half of the game though!

Most of my hours have been spent in survival mode. This is such an addicting game mode that I continue to come back to it over and over again over almost a decade.
The art style is beautiful and has held up very well to time. Everything looks like a rustic oil painting, cold, quiet, serene. It's at the same time comforting and peaceful as well as lonely and foreboding. The music is really lovely and blends perfectly with the setting.

Survival mode has a dedicated following for the past 10 years for a reason. It offers so much complexity and variance in the way it can be played and the vibe you want to play in. It has varying difficulty modes from "Pilgrim" to "Interloper".

"Pilgrim" gives a scenic, cozy experience. Spending time collecting, gathering, harvesting and exploring without the stress of hostile wildlife is what you get here. There are many many players who really don't enjoy the fear or stress of combat in videogames and this is perfect for that. Gather wood and make warm fires, pick berries and mushrooms for teas, and scour the landscape for unique cooking recipes.
